title: GLP-1 Weight Loss Drugs Linked to Sharply Lower Risk of Obesity-Related Cancers, Studies Show
excerpt: Multiple large-scale studies suggest medications like Ozempic and Mounjaro may reduce cancer risk by up to 65 percent for some tumour types, with researchers now investigating mechanisms beyond weight loss.
body:
• A study of 1.6 million diabetes patients found GLP-1 drugs reduced the risk of 10 out of 13 obesity-related cancers compared to insulin, with gallbladder cancer risk dropping 65 percent.
  • A separate analysis of 170,000 adults showed a 7 percent lower overall cancer incidence and 8 percent lower all-cause mortality in GLP-1 users, with women seeing the strongest benefit.
  • Duke University research in mice found GLP-1 drugs cut cancer risk so sharply it nearly matched lean animals, even on a high-fat diet, suggesting mechanisms beyond weight loss.
  • Researchers believe GLP-1 drugs may fight cancer through anti-inflammatory pathways and by directly targeting tumours expressing GLP-1 receptors.

What the Numbers Show

The evidence linking GLP-1 receptor agonists — the class of drugs behind Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro — to lower cancer risk has been building across multiple large studies, and the findings are striking.

In the largest retrospective study to date, researchers at Case Western Reserve University analysed health records of more than 1.6 million patients with type 2 diabetes. Patients taking GLP-1 drugs had significantly lower rates of 10 out of 13 obesity-associated cancers compared to those on insulin. The reductions were dramatic: gallbladder cancer risk dropped 65 percent, meningioma fell 63 percent, pancreatic cancer declined 59 percent and liver cancer was 53 percent lower.

A more recent observational study of 170,000 adults with diabetes and obesity, presented at the American Society of Clinical Oncology annual meeting, found a 7 percent reduction in obesity-related cancer incidence and an 8 percent lower all-cause mortality rate among GLP-1 users. The benefits were especially pronounced in women, who saw a 20 percent lower all-cause mortality rate.

Beyond Weight Loss

The simplest explanation — that weight loss itself reduces cancer pathways — accounts for part of the effect. Fat tissue is a source of oestrogen, which fuels certain breast cancers, and reducing it lowers that risk. But emerging research suggests GLP-1 drugs may be doing something more.

"These findings do not prove that GLP-1 drugs directly prevent cancer, but they strongly suggest that treating obesity may help lower cancer risk over time."

— Dr. Dawn Hershman, Columbia University

At Duke University, researcher Erika Crosby's team tested GLP-1 drugs in obese mice and found tumour growth slowed so dramatically that cancer risk nearly matched that of lean animals — even when the mice continued eating a high-fat diet. The finding points to anti-inflammatory mechanisms independent of weight loss.

GLP-1 receptors are found throughout the body, not just in the gut and pancreas. Activating them appears to dampen chronic inflammation — a key driver of tumour development — through multiple pathways, including effects on immune cells and vascular tissue.

Why This Matters for South Asians

South Asians face disproportionately high rates of type 2 diabetes and visceral obesity, often at lower body weights than Western populations. One in five American women aged 50 to 64 now uses a GLP-1 drug, and prescriptions are rising rapidly among Indian-origin populations in the U.S., UK and Gulf states.

Researchers caution that the studies are observational and cannot prove causation. Clinical trials specifically designed to test GLP-1 drugs as cancer-preventive agents are now being planned. In the meantime, the data adds a potentially significant dimension to the risk-benefit calculus for millions already taking these medications for diabetes and weight management.
nri_angle: With obesity and diabetes rates rising sharply among South Asians, GLP-1 drugs' potential anti-cancer benefits carry particular relevance for the Indian diaspora.
